articles.title_orig: Dow tumbles more than 600 points as oil prices rise and market sell-off hits most sectors
articles.title_zh: Dow tumbles more than 600 points as oil prices rise and market sell-off hits most sectors
articles.content_orig:
The Dow slid on Friday as a sell-off in tech in the prior session shifted to other areas of the market and U.S. oil prices topped $100 a barrel amid rising fears that the U.S.-Iran conflict would flare up again.
The Dow Jones Industrial Average dropped 652.82 points, or 1.23%, to settle at 52,215.16, while the S&P 500 slipped 0.52% to 7,623.68. The Nasdaq Composite lost 0.21% to close at 25,955.34.
More defensive stocks came under pressure on Friday, with the consumer staples, utilities and healthcare sectors all lower. Dow component American Express fell more than 3% after announcing it was cutting about 5% of its global workforce , citing the need to "prepare for AI." Caterpillar also edged down about 2%, while Goldman Sachs lost more than 1%, adding pressure to the 30-stock index.
On Thursday, many technology stocks had pulled back as traders assessed the impact of outsized corporate borrowing and rising rates on AI and other tech names. Microsoft ticked higher on Friday. However, chip stocks such as Micron Technology and Advanced Micro Devices made a stronger move, with gains of nearly 3% and almost 2%, respectively.
"For the last two weeks, investors have been sprinting from tech stocks and data center beneficiary stocks to safe stuff, and eventually, you run out of people willing to do that sprint, and that's what today looks like and feels like," Jed Ellerbroek, portfolio manager at Argent Capital Management, told CNBC.
Ellerbroek added that tech companies' earnings have proven strong this season, giving investors a reason to embrace tech stocks and focus less on emotion-based flights to safety.
"Emotion and fear play a really big role," the investor said. But, "we've gotten a few tech companies' [latest quarterly financial reports] and their earnings results have been good."
The 10-year Treasury yield was at around 4.999%, up more than 4 basis points on the day. The benchmark yield had fallen below the key 5% level on Thursday for the first time in a month as investors grew cautious about the massive borrowing that is underway to finance the building of AI data centers.
Oil prices also rose on Friday, further pressuring stocks. West Texas Intermediate futures were up 3.8% to settle at $103.27 per barrel. Brent crude prices rose 3.1% to end the session at $116.72 for the highest settle since April. The gains follow reports that the U.S. and Israel may be drawing up plans for renewed attacks on Iran as part of the regional war that started in late February. Iran has countered that it is prepared to strike back as well.
On the week, the S&P 500 lost 0.5%, and the Nasdaq shed 0.7%. The Dow gained 0.4% in the period.
The three major stock indexes ended Friday's session with losses.
The Dow Jones Industrial Average shed 1.23%, or 652.82 points, to finish at 52,215.16. The S&P 500 ended down 0.52% at 7,623.68. The Nasdaq Composite closed down 0.21% at 25,955.34.
Shares of discount retailers are lower today after analysts at Wells Fargo warned in a note that rising diesel prices could pressure profits through the second half of the year and into 2027.
With third-quarter diesel prices up about 60% year-over-year, analysts estimate the average hit to operating margin will rise to about 27 basis points from 18 basis points in the second quarter. The drag on earnings per share is expected to more than double to 6.2%.
Dollar Tree and Dollar General are down around 5% in midday trading while Five Below and TJX Companies are both down more than 1% on the day. Wells Fargo says Dollar Tree is the most exposed, historically seeing a larger drag than peers when diesel spikes. They estimate the higher fuel costs will weigh on third-quarter profit by about $25 million, or 50 basis points of margin.
The increased costs could mean additional pressure on retail inflation.
Bank of America raised its price target on ServiceNow to $180, implying roughly 15% upside from Thursday's close.
BofA analyst Tal Liani reiterated his buy rating ahead of the company's third-quarter earnings on October 28, citing growing demand for its artificial intelligence offerings.
"We believe ServiceNow's AI could see broader adoption and incremental spend, which should support durable revenue growth," Liani wrote in a Friday note.
The bank's October CIO survey showed that nearly 36% of respondents expect to allocate more than 10% of their software budgets to AI, while nearly 55% said they were likely or very likely to use ServiceNow for back-office AI applications.
The analyst expects third-quarter subscription revenue to grow nearly 21% year over year as IT, customer service, and security adopt new AI products and automation tools.
Uranium, nuclear and clean energy exchange-traded funds all fell to 52-week lows on Friday, while the largest fossil fuel producers in the nation touched all-time highs.
Global X Uranium ETF and Sprott Uranium Miners ETF both dropped to their lowest levels since June 2025, while the VanEck Uranium and Nuclear ETF was at its lowest since May 2025. Of the stocks inside those ETFs, Centrus Energy , Oklo , NuScale Power , Energy Fuels and BWX Technologies were also at 52-week lows Friday.
Clean energy ETFs saw losses, too. Invesco Solar ETF and Invesco WilderHill Clean Energy ETF were at their lowest since September and August last year, respectively, while individual stocks in the group, such as NextPower , Solv Energy , Rivian Automotive and Fluence Energy , also dropped to 52-week lows.
Meanwhile, ExxonMobil , Chevron and ConocoPhillips all traded at all-time highs on Friday.
— Scott Schnipper, Gina Francolla
In a Friday note to clients, Goldman Sachs posed some key questions about hyperscaler Oracle's AI strategy as pressures mount on the AI trade and investors grow increasingly wary to part with capital.
Analyst Gabriela Borges at Goldman said the conversation around Oracle is centering on monetization in proportion to capital expenditures; the sustainability of demand amid customer concentration; and the company's ability to execute despite political pressures facing the data center buildout.
Borges has a buy rating on the stock and a price target of $206, implying upside of 64.1% compared to a closing price recorded as $125.54.
Among the key risks to the company listed by Goldman are "intense capex investment cycle and financing needs."
"Oracle has outlined a FY27 financing framework supported by roughly $20bn of equity issuance (ATM program, already executed), $20 – 25 bn of customer prepayments ($11 bn as of 1Q), ~$20bn of debt issuance (expected in 2HFY27), with the remainder funded through operating cash flow," Borges wrote.
Stocks outside the AI trade are taking the lead.
The S&P 500 Excluding AI index closed Thursday up 12.4% this year, edging out the S&P 500's roughly 12% gain. The gap has converged largely in October.
The ex-AI index is up about 6.6% in October, while the S&P 500, weighed down by concerns around AI financing, is down roughly 0.4%.
The move suggests some leadership broadening beyond AI-linked mega cap names that have dominated in recent periods. By sector, Energy and Consumer Staples are each up double digits in October while Information Technology and Communication Services lead lower, each down more than 5%.
Morgan Stanley reduced its price target on CoreWeave to $70 from $99 Friday, citing mounting financial pressures the so-called neocloud company is facing. The new target still implies 26% upside from Thursday's close.
Shares of CoreWeave, down 2% on Friday, have sold off over the past week amid investor fears over its massive artificial intelligence-rated debt. Its bond yields have also jumped, while the spread on its credit default swaps — which are insurance against default — has widened to levels generally considered distressed.

articles.title_orig: Intermountain announces $150M Horowitz gift for Las Vegas children’s hospital project
articles.title_zh: Intermountain announces $150M Horowitz gift for Las Vegas children’s hospital project
articles.content_orig:
Felicia and Ben Horowitz are donating $150 million to help build Nevada’s first standalone children’s hospital, which will bear their names.
Intermountain Health announced the gift Friday, saying it is one of the largest publicly announced gifts ever made to a children’s hospital in the United States.
“At the heart of this gift are children and families,” said Felicia Horowitz in a statement. “Every parent wants to know that when their child needs care, the very best people and resources are there for them. Nevada has a responsibility to create a place where exceptional care and exceptional caregivers come together for its children. If we can help make that possible, the impact will be felt for generations.”
The Horowitzes are longtime Las Vegas residents. Ben Horowitz is the co-founder of venture capital firm Andreessen Horowitz. Felicia Horowitz is the chief executive officer of the Horowitz Family Foundation and is the founder and president of The Paid in Full Foundation, a nonprofit that supports hip-hop artists.
In October 2024, the site was unveiled for the children’s hospital, which will be built on around 34 acres at the 122-acre UNLV’s Harry Reid Research and Technology Park in the southwest valley. The hospital will open with around 200 beds, around 2,000 to 3,000 caregivers and cost over $1 billion.
‘New standard for children’s health’
At an event to announce the gift Friday at the future site of the hospital, Felicia and Ben Horowitz said they chose to help establish the facility because of a health scare with one of their children 30 years ago. Others also shared the importance of having a children’s hospital.
After they visited a colleague’s beach house while living in California, their then-toddler son began screaming and crying “uncontrollably” during the drive home, Ben Horowitz said.
After three misdiagnoses of the flu and being unable to keep anything down, their son was referred to Lucile Packard Children’s Hospital at Stanford in Palo Alto, California. Doctors discovered a hernia in his intestine that required emergency surgery. Without it, he could have died.
Felicia Horowitz looked to her husband after their son’s surgery and told him “one day I really want to do for other people, what Lucille Packard did for me, I want to build a children’s hospital,” Ben Horowitz recalled.
“I really never want anybody in Las Vegas to lose a child because we don’t have the right healthcare,” he said.
Felicia Horowitz said the $150 million gift is a thank you to the community. She also gave specific thanks to Gov. Joe Lombardo, saying “it’s because you and your leadership, the children of Nevada will finally have a place that they can call their own.”
“We want to thank the people who make the state work,” she said.
At the event, a close family friend of the Horowitzes, Steve Stoute, record executive and founder and CEO of United Masters and Translation, shared the story of his daughter, Phoenix.
After his wife was turned away from the emergency room in Florida, they traveled to New York to see a specialist. She was immediately diagnosed with a rare, life-threatening pregnancy complication. They then travelled back to Florida to receive care at the Holtz Children’s Hospital in Miami.
“You realize that the people who work in these children’s hospitals are angels, angels that are sent from God,” said Stoute.
Even Lombardo shared the story of his grandson who had en ear infection that was unable to be treated in Nevada.
“This is a new standard for children’s health, a transformational investment in Nevada’s future,” said Lombardo during the event. “A place where world-class talent can come together in service of one purpose: helping our children thrive.”
Intermountain Health officials also gave their thanks to Felicia and Ben Horowitz for the gift.
“Intermountain Health is proud to honor their noble intentions and philanthropic spirit by making this site home to the Intermountain Health Felicia and Ben Horowitz Children’s Hospital,” said David Flood, chief development officer and president of the Intermountain Foundation.
Prior to the gift from the Horowitzes, other Las Vegans have announced massive donations toward the construction of the hospital, which is anticipated to break ground at the end of October.
MGM Resorts International President and CEO Bill Hornbuckle and his wife, Wendy, were named last year as co-chairs of the Nevada Campaign for Kids, a philanthropic push to support construction of the children’s hospital.
In early October, Las Vegas-based homebuilder Larry Canarelli and his wife Heidi announced a $50 million gift to the children’s hospital. With the commitment, a tower at the Intermountain Health hospital will be named in their honor.
In August, the Raiders made the largest donation in team history , gifting Intermountain Health $25 million toward the construction of the children’s hospital. The contribution is made up of $10 million from the Raiders and $5 million each from team owners Mark Davis, Egon Durban and Michael Meldman.
Contact Emerson Drewes at edrewes@reviewjournal.com. Follow @EmersonDrewes on X.
Every October 12, the world marks World Arthritis Day. It’s easy to assume that visibility belongs to grandparents, but it belongs to children too, and the doctors who treat them are harder to find than almost any others in medicine.
The upscale development is being built near Whole Foods at The District at Green Valley Ranch.
The Hughes Center was long viewed as the valley’s top office district but is now laced with vacancies.
Management put on a free, instructor-led outdoor workout session to drum up interest in the new facility.
Plans have called for 1,480 homes in the community now called The Preserve.
The property is near Nellis Air Force Base and the Las Vegas Motor Speedway, as well as numerous warehouses and distribution centers.
The chief executive said the new name tells a site selector, chief executive, and others “exactly who we are and who we represent.”
Lennar Corp. held a ceremonial groundbreaking for a big project on Washington Avenue at Las Vegas Boulevard.
The veteran architect says the city’s future will depend on creating distinctive experiences, embracing the outdoors and preserving the magic that made Las Vegas unique.
Harry Reid International Airport plans to add 26 gates, reconfigure existing terminals and improve traffic flow while keeping operations running through a period of major Las Vegas growth and events.
Artemis Real Estate Partners picked up two big buildings in the remote Apex Industrial Park.

articles.title_orig: Trump and Burnham discuss North Sea oil, Ukraine and Falklands
articles.title_zh: Trump and Burnham discuss North Sea oil, Ukraine and Falklands
articles.content_orig:
US President Donald Trump has praised Prime Minister Andy Burnham for the UK government's decision to approve production from the North Sea's Jackdaw gas field.
He said he had spoken with Burnham, telling reporters on Friday that the decision would "make the UK a very rich country".
Trump said: "The other prime minister, the previous man, Starmer. He's a very nice man, but he never got it done, and this one is getting it."
The decision had been subject to intense debate around its environment and economic impact and came after years of legal challenges.
Burnham announced the decision to approve the drilling of the Jackdaw gas field earlier this week.
Jackdaw is situated 150 miles (241km) east of Aberdeen and is operated by Adura, a joint venture between Shell and Norwegian state energy firm Equinor.
Ministers said the first gas could be produced by the end of this month, helping heat millions of homes, and also announced the creation of a new energy wealth fund.
Environmental campaigners say the decision would hamper efforts to tackle climate change and make "no meaningful difference" to UK energy security.
Based on official forecasts for the amount of gas the UK will need over the next decade, that suggests Jackdaw has the potential to meet around 1.6% of total projected national gas demand between 2026 and 2036.
Operators say it could be connected to the Great British gas network within weeks and could produce gas for the next 11 years.
Trump responded to the decision on Friday, but appeared to confuse oil and gas.
He said: "They're opening up the North Sea oil. I've been after them to do that for two years."
Trump added: "Andy is getting it done, and I guess it's against the liberal principle, but he knows what's right. It's going to make UK a very wealthy country."
In a discussion on Friday, Burnham and Trump spoke about the decision to approve Jackdaw.
The two leaders "agreed on the significant benefits this will bring to the UK, boosting the economy and supporting jobs for British workers", a statement from Number 10 read.
It added that Trump and Burnham "welcomed the continued collaboration between UK and US companies, especially on nuclear power".
Earlier this week, on Wednesday, Trump said the decision was "great news for the wealth and prosperity" of the UK.
Writing on his Truth Social platform, Trump urged the UK to go "full blast" and called the North Sea "one of the greatest and most prosperous areas of oil in the world".
A decision is yet to be taken on whether production can begin at Rosebank, the UK's largest known untapped oil field, which is located off the coast of Shetland in the North Atlantic.
Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch accused the prime minister of "dithering" on Jackdaw and said a ban on new oil and gas licences should be repealed.
However, Burnham said her party had "messed up" the original decision by not giving any regard to climate obligations - things he said "have to be considered in the round".
Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh said gas from Jackdaw would be in homes and businesses this month, but that it would not lower energy bills this winter.
She said the decision was "compatible" with legally binding climate commitments, adding:  "We remain resolute in ending new licences for oil and gas and achieving net zero by 2050."
Environmental groups have criticised the Jackdaw approval. Areeba Hamid, the co-executive director of Greenpeace, said it was "the wrong decision" in terms of lowering energy bills, providing energy security, and addressing climate change.
Meanwhile, Oxfam said the government had "drilled straight through the UK's climate commitments".
During their Friday talks, Trump and Burnham spoke about the Falkland Islands and the Sea Lion oilfield project, a joint venture between British and Israeli companies.
In September, the Argentinian government threatened to impose economic sanctions on firms exploiting oil close to the Falkland Islands, and earlier this month, it began legal action to stop the exploration of oil and gas fields.
Burnham raised the "economic consequences of Argentina's coercive measures for the UK and US and reiterated the importance of respecting the Islanders' right to develop their natural resources", Downing Street said.
The two leaders also discussed Ukraine, with the prime minister underlining the importance for Ukraine "to have full access to Starlink so they can continue to defend themselves against Russia's full-scale invasion", according to Number 10.
Starlink technology is a satellite system owned by Elon Musk's SpaceX company which Ukraine has relied upon during the war.
In recent days, Ukraine has been recording issues with the network , according to sources within the defence ministry. This has affected the country's ability to use attack drones and co-ordinate defensive operations.
The Downing Street statement added: "The Prime Minister recognised the work of President Trump to bring Putin to the negotiation table and the leaders agreed to work together, alongside international partners to bring an end to the bloodshed."

articles.title_orig: Ukrainian negotiator says local humanitarian ceasefire with Russia will start Tuesday
articles.title_zh: Ukrainian negotiator says local humanitarian ceasefire with Russia will start Tuesday
articles.content_orig:
WASHINGTON (AP) — First lady Melania Trump has brokered a coming ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine in the ravaged, Russian-occupied Ukrainian city of Oleshky so that humanitarian aid can be delivered and civilians can be evacuated from a place she said is “on the brink of disaster.”
The localized ceasefire is set to begin next week.
Ukrainian, Russian and U.S. negotiators reached a deal Friday to provide humanitarian relief to the Russian-occupied town of Oleshky in the war-divided region of Kherson in southern Ukraine.
Melania Trump, who worked with officials from both countries on a separate matter, initiated talks about Oleshky after learning about the situation at one of her events during the U.N. General Assembly session in September, the White House said in announcing her involvement.
She and a representative worked directly with Russian and Ukrainian leadership to define the terms of the ceasefire, the White House said.
Ukraine’s top negotiator in the effort told The Associated Press that a local ceasefire with Russia will start Tuesday — two days before the mission begins — and last several days.
Dmytro Lubinets, the Ukrainian ombudsman and his country’s chief negotiator in the talks, said the ceasefire would take effect across the Kherson region and neighboring areas essential to the operation. He added the initiative could act as a model for future humanitarian missions.
Russian officials also confirmed the agreement.
Lubinets earlier Friday thanked Melania Trump and said the deal would be tough to accomplish. He said the agreement calls for a ceasefire, followed by the delivery of much-needed humanitarian aid. Lastly, civilians will be allowed to leave Oleshky, he said in a video message posted online.
“The operation will be carried out gradually and is extremely challenging to implement,” Lubinets said.
Lubinets said the operation would involve removing mines on the way to Oleshky before the physical delivery of humanitarian supplies and the arranging of evacuations.
He gave no further details on how the ceasefire or the aid mission would be monitored or implemented, citing the sensitivity of the negotiations. He declined to comment when asked if Melania Trump would travel to Ukraine.
“When Melania Trump learned about the situation in Oleshky, the negotiation process began under her coordination,” he said. “For several weeks, we discussed many questions, initiatives and ideas. We established new approaches, mechanisms and tools to do everything possible to help civilians in Oleshky survive.”
Russia’s chief of the general staff, Gen. Valery Gerasimov, said Russian forces “will cease fire on the Kherson axis” starting at 4 a.m. Tuesday in Moscow” — or late Monday in the United States — “in connection with the humanitarian operation near Oleshky.”
Russian forces will also carry out “engineering reconnaissance” and ensure “safe movement of the humanitarian convoy” into the city, Gerasimov said.
Russia’s human rights ombudswoman, Yana Lantratova, confirmed that Melania Trump had brokered an agreement on “organizing a humanitarian mission” in Oleshky. Lantratova, who said she participated in negotiations, said providing such assistance is Russia’s priority.
The first step will be to clarify what people need and organize the delivery of food, medicine, hygiene products and other essentials, Lantratova said in an online statement. Safe passage will be guaranteed for anyone who wants to leave the combat zone, she said, adding that it will require abiding by the ceasefire and creating safe conditions for humanitarian vehicles.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said Moscow was grateful to the first lady. He said Russian President Vladimir Putin and President Donald Trump had recently discussed the effort.
Peskov said “those who want to leave it would be able to do so.” He would not say whether they would be taken to Russia- or Ukraine-held territory. He also demurred when asked how long the evacuation will last, saying only it would most likely take several days.
Melania Trump has made helping children in conflict zones one of her signature issues in her husband’s second term. She hosted a U.N. Security Council meeting on the issue earlier this year, and last year wrote Putin about efforts to reunite families with children who have been displaced by the war. She has helped reunite nearly three dozen children, according to her senior adviser, Marc Beckman.
“What she wants to do is save children, and that’s her focus,” the president told reporters at the White House.
Beckman portrayed the first lady’s work on the ceasefire as an extension of her efforts to help reunite Russian and Ukrainian children with their families after they were separated by Russia’s war against Ukraine.
The development comes as tensions have increased to new highs between the Trump administration and Ukraine’s government. Kyiv has faced restrictions on the satellite internet system it relies on to knock down Russian attacks, with Trump and other top U.S. officials sending mixed messages about who was responsible for throttling the Elon Musk-made Starshield system.
Trump also recently waived new Russia sanctions , reached an agreement with Russia to import diesel fuel and pushed Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy to make a deal to end the war that Russia began in February 2022. In renewed efforts to revive the peace process , Trump envoy Steve Witkoff traveled to Norway this week for talks with Zelenskyy before meeting Putin in St. Petersburg, Russia.
Zelenskyy did not mention the ceasefire in Oleshky during a remote appearance at the Hudson Institute, a Washington think tank. He did note that American Patriot missile interceptors were still on hold and Starshield and Starlink speed limits were still in place.
He also spoke of the importance of the United States to renewed diplomatic efforts to end the war, including a possible joint meeting with Trump and Putin.
Food and medical supplies have been scarce for months in Oleshky, which sits on the Dnipro River that separates Ukrainian forces from the city’s Russian occupiers. There is no electricity, heat or running water. Roads leading from town are mined and dotted with burned-out cars. Drones buzz overhead.
Once a city of about 24,000 residents, Oleshky was captured by Moscow’s forces on the first day of their full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022. Its buildings were shelled and burned, and its infrastructure damaged. In June 2023, floodwaters inundated the city after the Kakhovka Dam collapsed from an explosion that an Associated Press investigation found was likely caused by the Russian military. Hundreds of residents were killed.
Those left in the city along Ukraine’s southeastern front face death from hunger or disease as another harsh winter looms. Ukraine has appealed repeatedly for a local ceasefire to organize evacuations. Russia, as the occupying power, is obligated by international law to ensure civilians under its control have what they need to survive.
Associated Press writers Konstantin Toropin and Darlene Superville in Washington, Volodymyr Yurchuk, Derek Gatopoulos and Susie Blann in Kyiv, Ukraine, and Dasha Litvinova in Tallinn, Estonia, contributed to this report.

articles.title_orig: Wolves Descend on Finnish Villages After Google Hacked Down 1,300 Acres of Habitat to Make Room for AI Data Centers
articles.title_zh: Wolves Descend on Finnish Villages After Google Hacked Down 1,300 Acres of Habitat to Make Room for AI Data Centers
articles.content_orig:
Earlier in October, Finnish authorities ordered Google’s affiliate data center developer Tuike Finland Oy to immediately suspend the illegal cutting of some 1,300 acres of forest. The tech giant was given a week to draft a report explaining its actions, which soon became a flashpoint for Europe’s growing outrage over the data center boom.
As the anger grew, reporters descended on the scene — and what they found is a clear-cut example of the AI revolution’s impact on the environment.
New reporting by the Guardian shed fresh light on the impacts of Google’s deforestation. After the 1,300 acres of pristine boreal forests were reduced to tracts of mud and stumps, fauna which once called the woods home has been forced to vacate.
In the felling-site near the Finnish village of Otanmäki, the ensuing loss of prey has forced packs of wolves to search for food elsewhere: nearby villages.
“We had wolves coming into the village because all the wild animals moved out of the forest,” 53-year-old Otanmäki resident Anni Ranta told the Guardian . “They fled.”
Though Ranta’s family has called the area home for generations, the tumult has her considering whether to move out of Otanmäki for good.
“I don’t want them here,” she continued, speaking of Google’s data centers. “I don’t want them in Finland at all. I don’t like the whole idea of AI and the world changing and the way it’s changing. It’s going too fast, too soon.”
Antti Jakonen, a resident of Muhos, put it in even starker terms. “It has been done in the wrong way. American style. No sense. No sense at all,” he told the Guardian .
Sure enough, back in Google’s home country, data center developers are increasingly duking it out with the natural world — and winning handily.
In West Virginia, a grove of critically endangered Chestnut trees is under threat of being bulldozed to make way for a new Anthropic hyperscale facility. Outside of Fort Wayne, a chunk of Indiana’s once-bountiful wetlands is being tilled to fit a new Google data center. In Southern New Jersey, a data center operator was recently slapped with a $1 million fine after inspectors uncovered 62 illegal gas generators belching exhaust into the surrounding environment.
Wherever in the world data centers go up, it seems the destruction of natural resources is inevitable — and increasingly difficult for humanity to ignore.

articles.title_orig: Trump's executive order targets mortgage insurance, refinance costs. What it means for borrowers
articles.title_zh: Trump's executive order targets mortgage insurance, refinance costs. What it means for borrowers
articles.content_orig:
President Donald Trump has signed an executive order aimed at housing affordability with days to go before the midterm elections.
The multipart executive order published on Thursday aims to reduce costs for title and mortgage insurance and promote more affordable manufactured housing. Trump said he wanted to see new technologies that use artificial intelligence, or "super intelligence," to accelerate the housing market.
"The American Dream of homeownership is a vital pillar of our great country," the order states. "It is the policy of my Administration to reduce regulatory barriers to mortgage origination and costs impeding homeownership"
This comes amid a year Americans are concerned about housing affordability. The housing market has been hammered by high interest rates and inflation hitting costs of materials and labor. Mortgage rates are likely to remain near decade highs for the near term.
This year, Congress passed the 21st Century Road to Housing Act after months of sometimes-contentious negotiations . The bill's 45 provisions are aimed at cutting red tape and encouraging the construction of more homes. Trump refused to sign the bill, though it still became law.
Among the ideas in the bill are a pilot program for federal housing agencies to cancel "excessive" mortgage insurance for select borrowers "who appear to satisfy equity and other requirements."
Another provision would establish a task force aimed at promoting innovation in manufactured housing, to be chaired by Federal Housing Finance Agency Director Bill Pulte and Secretary of Housing and Urban Development Scott Turner .
Trump "is committing to bring even more innovative and affordable housing solutions to market for the American people,” Turner said in a statement.
“For decades, home building has been crippled by regulatory red tape, but the Task Force on Manufactured Housing Innovation can usher in the next generation of housing by modernizing standards and speeding up approvals across government,” Turner added.
Pulte posted to X that the order was "the greatest Housing Executive Order in History" and said it could save "thousands" of dollars for millions of Americans.
The task force would incorporate over government leaders and create recommendations for how to accelerate innovation in the homebuilding industry.
The order directs FHFA to establish a pilot program for Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac aimed at reducing mortgage insurance costs for homeowners.
This program will use automated valuation models to periodically assess home values and proactively cancel mortgage insurance for borrowers who have met the necessary equity requirements, eliminating the need for excessive documentation and costly appraisals.
Typically, homeowners with at least 20% equity in their home are not required to carry mortgage insurance, which protects the lender in the event of a borrower default.
To lower costs for homeowners who refinance their mortgage, the order also directs the FHFA to expand a program that accepts automated title reviews in place of traditional lender’s title insurance policies.
As well, it seeks to waive appraisals and documentation requirements for certain refinances while ensuring that all cost savings are directly passed on to the borrowers.
In a statement , Shannon McGahn , chief advocacy officer at the National Association of Realtors®, lauded the administration's efforts to promote housing affordability.
"We appreciate the President’s continued focus on this critical issue and look forward to reviewing the Administration’s proposals in greater detail," McGahn said in the statement. "We also look forward to working with federal policymakers to advance practical solutions that lower costs, expand housing opportunities, and help more Americans achieve the dream of homeownership.”
Bill Owens , chairman of the National Association of Home Builders, says the group "commends President Trump and his administration for making housing a national priority."
"The president’s executive order will help reduce single-family housing and mortgage costs," says Owens. "We urge the administration to continue its efforts to reduce regulatory burdens to make housing more affordable for all Americans.”
Bob Broeksmit , president and CEO of the Mortgage Bankers Association, says that the group's lender members "welcome these latest initiatives to reduce the costs of refinancing and expand innovative manufactured housing options for potential homebuyers."
“MBA appreciates the Trump administration’s continued focus on lowering housing costs by reducing unnecessary regulatory burdens, streamlining mortgage processes, and promoting competition across the housing market," says Broeksmit. “MBA will continue to identify and advocate for additional ways to help homebuyers navigate today’s higher interest rate environment and to work with the Administration and Congress to advance policies that deliver meaningful results for homeowners, homebuyers, and renters.”
American Land Title Association CEO Chris Morton says that efforts to improve housing affordability are "critical." But he warned that any effort to bring title insurance costs down "must also preserve the essential consumer safeguards that protect Americans' most valuable assets.
"Fraud is unaffordable, and the threats facing homeowners are growing," says Morton. "Now more than ever, we need to ensure that efforts to lower housing costs do not shift significant financial risks onto American families or the broader housing finance system."
Tristan Navera is a senior reporter on housing policy, covering trends and solutions in the housing market from Washington, DC. He was previously a senior reporter at Bloomberg Law, and before that covered real estate for the Washington Business Journal. Earlier in his career, he spent a decade reporting on business and real estate in Dayton and Columbus, OH. A Cincinnati native, he holds a journalism degree from Ohio University.

articles.title_orig: Report: Apple gains ground in China as smartphone shipments hit 14-year low in Q3
articles.title_zh: Report: Apple gains ground in China as smartphone shipments hit 14-year low in Q3
articles.content_orig:
Rising memory prices continue to weigh on the global smartphone market, with shipments in China alone falling 10% year over year in Q3. Here are the details.
A few days ago, IDC reported that smartphone shipments in China fell 15.4% year over year in Q3 2026, with Apple increasing its share of that total to 17.8% despite a 4.3% decline in iPhone shipments.
The report echoed the broader global trend, with IDC estimating that worldwide smartphone shipments fell a record 22% year over year during the quarter, while Apple recorded the smallest decline among the top five manufacturers, at just 4%.
Now, a new report from Counterpoint Research paints a similar picture of China’s smartphone market in Q3, although its estimates differ somewhat from IDC’s.
According to the report, smartphone shipments in China hit a 14-year low during Q3 2026, with a 10% decline year over year.
Apple, on the other hand, accounted for 19.5% of smartphone shipments in China during the period, a 4.8-percentage-point increase year over year. The company was second only to Huawei, which held a 21.3% share, up 5.3 percentage points from a year earlier.
In fact, these were the only two among the top six brands to gain shipment share year over year, with vivo down 2.8 percentage points to 15.2%, OPPO down 1.3 points to 15.1%, Xiaomi down 1.6 points to 13.5%, HONOR down 2.2 points to 12.7%, and other manufacturers collectively down 2 points to 2.8%.
Notably, Apple went from sixth to second place in overall shipments, which Counterpoint attributes in part to the strong launch of the iPhone 18 Pro series:
Apple ranked second with a 19.5% market share in Q3. The iPhone 18 Pro series saw a strong launch in China, with sales in the first three weeks up 23.5% YoY compared with the iPhone 17 Pro series. The delayed launch of the base iPhone 18 may have encouraged some consumers to trade up to the Pro models, supporting their early sales momentum.
Looking ahead, Counterpoint noted that rising smartphone prices are leading consumers to delay upgrades, wait for promotional periods, or turn to refurbished devices, potentially putting further pressure on demand in Q4.
To check out Counterpoint Research’s full report, follow this link .

articles.title_zh: Sony Retires Its Last 4K Blu-ray Player in Japan, PS5 Is All That's Left
articles.content_orig:
The latest hi-fi, home cinema and tech news, reviews, buying advice and deals, direct to your inbox.
Your newsletter sign-up was successful
Just when it looked like a 4K Blu-ray revival was in full gear, Sony could be about to bring the occasion to a crashing halt.
Reports suggest the firm is ending production of its final commercial model, the UBP-X700/K, despite only launching it just over a year ago.
Kunkoku , a Japanese blog dedicated to Sony products and a Sony retail partner, reports (via FlatpanelsHD ) that Sony has "ended shipments of its Ultra HD Blu-ray player", with sales of the UBP-X700/K ceasing once stock runs out.
Visiting the Sony Japan online store reveals that the player is already out of stock, so it may already be too late for those looking to purchase the Blu-ray player in Japan.
This could leave the PlayStation 5 as the company's final remaining device capable of playing 4K Blu-ray discs.
But that will be of little comfort to physical media fans, as we know from Sony's previous announcement that future PlayStation consoles will not support physical discs.
On a wider scale, Panasonic could be the only remaining mainstream manufacturer to continue producing 4K disc players, with new players, such as Krovatar, and enthusiast manufacturers, including Magnetar, filling in the gaps.

articles.title_orig: SpaceX Just Made Cell Towers Cool Again. Verizon, AT&T, and T-Mobile Are Paying the Price
articles.title_zh: SpaceX Just Made Cell Towers Cool Again. Verizon, AT&T, and T-Mobile Are Paying the Price
articles.content_orig:
There were some big moves in telecommunications stocks on Friday. On one hand, shares of cell tower owners Crown Castle ( CCI +9.06% ) and American Tower ( AMT +4.08% ) soared, with shares up by about 9% and 4%, respectively, as of midday. On the other hand, the three largest wireless carriers plunged, with Verizon ( VZ -1.20% ) , AT&T ( T -7.96% ) , and T-Mobile ( TMUS -7.71% ) all deep in the red.
Both moves are due to one company, SpaceX ( SPCX +1.89% ) . On Thursday evening, Bloomberg reported that SpaceX is in talks to secure at least 80,000 cell sites across the United States as it aims to become the fourth nationwide wireless carrier. For context, 80,000 sites would represent about half of all the purpose-built cell towers in the U.S., so it would be a pretty big move.
Image source: Getty Images.
This is the second time in October that SpaceX has sent shockwaves through the telecom industry. First, on Oct. 9, SpaceX agreed to buy $8 billion in low-frequency wireless spectrum, and telecom stocks plunged. So, will SpaceX truly boost the tower companies and cost the telecom leaders money?
First, a little context on how the cell tower business works. The owner builds a tower and then rents space on it to wireless carriers, typically under long-term leases. Next time you drive by a cell tower, take a look at the top. You'll probably see several rings of transmission equipment, and each of those represents a tenant. Since the tower is already standing, adding tenants produces extra revenue with very little additional cost.
NYSE · As of 4:00 PM ET 10/23/26
Ever since Sprint was acquired by T-Mobile, the tower industry has essentially had three wireless customers . The majority of Crown Castle's rent comes from AT&T, Verizon, and T-Mobile. A well-capitalized fourth player would mean more tenants per tower.
This is also a notable expansion of SpaceX's plans. Although the company has made its telecom network ambitions known for some time, as recently as August, management described its network as small cells mounted on rooftops (not traditional towers). But without getting too technical, the low-band spectrum it bought makes large towers far more useful, so it makes sense to add them to the plan.
Of course, this isn't the first time a "fourth carrier" has emerged. Just a few years ago, Dish Network signed long-term tower leases to build its own 5G network. To make a long story short, Dish's parent company sold most of its spectrum in 2025 and began shutting down the network. Of course, SpaceX is a far more deep-pocketed tenant and could easily afford to build a nationwide network.
SpaceX is certainly a threat to the big three wireless carriers, but the recent sell-off appears a bit overdone. After all, SpaceX would be starting with no wireless customers at all, it holds less spectrum than any of the others, and its service isn't expected to launch commercially until late 2027. And building a competitive network would be a multiyear process at a minimum.
Let's be clear. SpaceX could certainly pressure the three major wireless carriers over time, but this isn't exactly a death sentence for them either. All have existed in the past with a fourth competitor (Sprint), and pricing power hasn't changed that much since the number dropped to three.
If you're thinking about buying tower owners as a momentum play or telecoms at a discount, it might be a smart idea to be patient. For one thing, although Crown Castle was specifically mentioned as a company SpaceX was in talks with, there isn't a signed contract or any official management acknowledgment yet. And the telecom sell-off may be overdone, as all that is happening right now is that a potential competitor (who would be starting from scratch) is negotiating with landlords.
In a nutshell, the market is pricing in a deal that hasn't happened yet, and the reaction on both the tower owner and wireless carrier side may be a bit overdone. I'm keeping an eye on some of the stocks involved, but I'm waiting for further official developments before making any moves.

articles.title_orig: Microsoft says its AI tool outperforms generalist doctors in complex diagnoses
articles.title_zh: Microsoft says its AI tool outperforms generalist doctors in complex diagnoses
articles.content_orig:
Apollon Wealth Management CIO Eric Sterner discusses how technology is driving gains in the healthcare sector on ‘The Claman Countdown.’
Microsoft researchers said in a study that a new artificial intelligence (AI) tool that can diagnose patients step by step, as a doctor would, was more than twice as accurate as general physicians at solving complex medical cases.
The study, published Thursday in Science , said the AI model takes a different approach to diagnosing medical issues than most other models that seek to address those issues.
Microsoft said the AI model identifies and coordinates the questions that should be asked of a patient and the exams and tests that should be ordered using an "orchestrator" that organizes how AI will tackle a problem by employing a simulated panel of clinical experts collaborating to solve diagnostic cases, the report said.
By contrast, existing AI models typically take an all-at-once approach that examines all of a patient's symptoms, lab results and imaging studies to generate a diagnosis.
MICROSOFT PRESIDENT SAYS AI FACES FEWER SAFETY RULES THAN MILK IN CALL FOR GLOBAL REGULATION
Microsoft's research showed the AI orchestrator was more effective in diagnosing complex cases at a lower cost. (Nvidia)
While the orchestrator coordinates the steps to reach a diagnosis , the AI model first decides what questions to ask about the patient's medical history and identifies significant findings in the physical exam.
Based on what it learns from that process, it decides which tests to order, considers the results and orders further testing as appropriate. While those tasks are ongoing, the AI model is updating its working hypotheses and plans.
MICROSOFT UNVEILS CODE OF CONDUCT FOR AI MODELS AS SAFETY CONCERNS MOUNT
Microsoft will next test the AI model and orchestrator in an emergency room setting. (Philips)
The tool also outperformed human physicians when it was presented with scenarios drawn from a major database of emergency room admissions. Researchers said assessments comparing these types of older systems to human doctors usually use multiple choice questions.
"AI has become very good at getting a 100% pass rate on those," said Dr. Dominic King, the corporate vice president of the health unit at Microsoft AI, which is developing the new technology. "But, of course, that's not real-world. No patient ever came to see me with a nice summary."
The researchers tasked the model with diagnosing over 300 highly unusual and confusing medical dilemmas and found that the model using the diagnostic orchestrator was over twice as accurate at "working up" the patient and determining the diagnosis as general physicians using textbooks and the internet.
ANTHROPIC SILENT ON WHETHER IT WILL DISTRIBUTE SHARES TO AMERICANS FOLLOWING MUSK SPACEX PLEDGE
Researchers also found that diagnostic processes cost less when the orchestrator designs the work-ups than when human doctors do.
"We're not just measuring the accuracy of the systems. We're also measuring how judiciously and carefully it goes through a diagnostic work-up," said Harsha Nori, head of AI at Microsoft AI Health.
The Microsoft research team's next test will occur through a collaboration with Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center in Boston, where it will evaluate the tool's ability to triage patients in emergency department waiting rooms.

articles.title_orig: Meta faces massive AI bills and legal troubles. Mark Zuckerberg keeps finding ways to come out on top.
articles.title_zh: Meta faces massive AI bills and legal troubles. Mark Zuckerberg keeps finding ways to come out on top.
articles.content_orig:
This is read by an automated voice. Please report any issues or inconsistencies here .
See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search. Set us as preferred
Meta’s Chief Executive Mark Zuckerberg has wielded enormous power over the social media empire he built more than two decades ago, leading the California juggernaut through major scandals, scrutiny and technological shifts.
But the 42-year-old tech mogul considered leaving the state because he feared that a ballot measure to impose a one-time 5% tax on the assets of California billionaires could reduce the amount of control he has over Meta, a recent regulatory filing shows. Meta’s board struck a deal so he would stay in California. Meta is the parent company of Facebook, Instagram and WhatsApp.
The filing highlights how one of the world’s wealthiest people, whose net worth totals more than $200 billion, is bracing for the possibility that California voters pass Proposition 40, a wealth tax proposal that would primarily be used to fund healthcare.
Although supporters say the fear that billionaires will flee the state are overblown, the ultrawealthy have made moves to potentially avoid paying the tax or are funding campaigns to defeat it.
Prop 40, which would tax the assets of California billionaires to mostly fund healthcare, has divided Democratic politicians, labor unions and other groups.
Zuckerberg’s influence over Meta is partly tied to how the company structures its stock. Zuckerberg holds roughly 60% of voting power over Meta even though he only owns about 13% of the company’s total shares.
Meta has a dual-class share structure, dividing the stock into Class A shares with one vote each and Class B shares with 10 votes each. Zuckerberg holds a large amount of Class B stock, which gives him majority control over company decisions.
If the wealth tax proposal passes, Zuckerberg is worried that it could reduce his voting power, according to the filing. The tech executive makes an annual salary of $1, so most of his wealth is linked to his stake in Meta. If he had to sell his Class B shares to pay the tax, that would reduce his voting majority in the company, according to the filing.
In September, he told Meta’s board that he planned to list his Palo Alto home for sale, pressuring board members to find a solution.
On Wednesday, Meta announced a new class of stock with no voting rights called Class C that would take effect in January. As part of the deal, Zuckerberg could sell or transfer up to 20% of Class C stock so his voting majority doesn’t decrease even if he has to pay the tax.
“Mr. Zuckerberg’s continued leadership role in our Company, and his continuing presence at the Company’s headquarters in California, is critical at this current inflection point for the Company and the tech industry in order to continue to provide value-maximization for all shareholders,” the filing said.
Since the company’s public debut, its share price has risen more than 1,700%, outperforming the S&P 500.
In Meta’s third-quarter earnings call Wednesday, Chief Financial Officer Susan Li said creating a new class of nonvoting stock benefits the company in various ways, including “capital raising, employee compensation, acquisitions, other general corporate purposes.”
“We believe this share class will maintain our founder-led structure. It will expand our funding tools and give us flexibility to invest behind the unprecedented momentum we’re seeing across every part of our business driven by AI,” she said.
Meta has roughly 66,700 workers globally. Its sprawling headquarters is in Menlo Park.
Some billionaires such as Anduril co-founder Palmer Luckey, Ripple co-founder Chris Larsen and Google co-founder Sergey Brin have opposed the wealth tax proposal. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, on the other hand, has said he doesn’t mind paying more taxes.
The Service Employees International Union-United Healthcare Workers West is backing the wealth tax proposal and says it applies to roughly 200 billionaires who have resided in California as of January 1, 2026, and could raise $100 billion.
More than $300 million has been contributed to fight the billionaire tax, including two propositions that could block it if they gather more votes. Although stock prices fluctuate, Zuckerberg could face a tax liability of roughly $12 billion based on his net worth.
In 2015, Zuckerberg and his wife, Dr. Priscilla Chan, pledged to give away 99% of his Facebook shares over their lifetimes when they celebrated the birth of their first daughter.
The couple created the Chan Zuckerberg Initiative, a philanthropic organization whose efforts include curing, managing and preventing all diseases. Although Zuckerberg lives in Palo Alto, he also owns real estate elsewhere, including in Hawaii, Washington, D.C. and Ireland.

articles.title_orig: Moderna mRNA vaccine almost halves the risk of skin cancer returning
articles.title_zh: Moderna mRNA vaccine almost halves the risk of skin cancer returning
articles.content_orig:
Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain
            the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in
            Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles
            and JavaScript.
Severe sunburn increases the risk of developing melanoma, the most serious type of skin cancer. Credit: Olga Pankova/Getty
A personalized mRNA vaccine reduced the risk of skin cancer returning or the recipient dying by 42% when used alongside an immunotherapy drug, according to long-awaited results for what could become the first approved mRNA vaccine for cancer.
Oncologists regard a risk reduction of 10% as substantial, says Kristen Radford, an immunotherapist at Mater Research in Brisbane. A risk reduction of more than 40% “would send many researchers over the Moon”, adds Seth Cheetham, a geneticist at the University of Queensland in Brisbane, Australia.
The personalized vaccine, called intismeran, is not designed to prevent skin cancer, or melanoma, from developing in the first place, but to stop it returning in people who have already undergone surgery to remove tumours.
Anticipation for the trial results has been building since August, when the vaccine’s developers — Merck, based in Rahway, New Jersey, and Moderna, which is headquartered in Cambridge, Massachusetts — announced early positive results . Data from the phase III trial will be presented at the European Society for Medical Oncology meeting in Madrid on 24 October. But when data were leaked online on 22 October, the companies released the key results.
The stock price for Moderna, a pioneer in mRNA vaccine technology, had been rising since the August announcement, but dropped by around 25% after the leak. Health-care financial analyst Evan Seigerman at BMO Capital Markets in New York City told media company Forbes that such reactions in the stock market probably reflect “inflated expectation into the full data release, rather than a true indictment on the efficacy of the combo therapy”.
The intismeran trial enrolled 1,137 people with moderate to advanced melanoma across 157 centres. Participants were randomly assigned to receive either a tailor-made vaccine (intismeran) alongside the immunotherapy drug pembrolizumab — which is already used to treat melanoma — or pembrolizumab plus an inactive placebo. Trial leader Georgina Long, an oncologist at Melanoma Institute Australia in Sydney, says participants have so far been followed for around 25 months and will continue to be monitored for several years to determine whether the vaccine improves overall survival. She adds that the therapy did not result in any major harmful side effects.
Roughly 15 years ago, people with advanced melanoma typically survived for only months. Today, nearly 55% are effectively cured with targeted drugs or immunotherapies, says Long. The combination of intismeran and pembrolizumab is designed for people whose cancer could return after surgery and who do not respond to immunotherapy alone, she says.
Jessamy Tiffen, a cancer geneticist at the Centenary Institute in Sydney, says that the trial results are exciting, but that only time will tell how effective the treatment is beyond two years. “Cancer cells also have an insidious ability to adapt and evade whatever treatment we throw at them,” she says. Furthermore, some people did not respond to the vaccine, she says.
Long says that her team will conduct a statistical analysis to identify who is most likely to benefit from the treatment.
To develop intismeran, Long and her colleagues sequenced DNA from a sample of each participant’s tumour to identify mutations in the cancer cells. These mutations can give rise to proteins called neoantigens, which help to distinguish cancer cells from healthy ones.

articles.title_orig: ‘Black October’: cybersecurity experts sound the alarm over new era of AI-enabled hacking
articles.title_zh: ‘Black October’: cybersecurity experts sound the alarm over new era of AI-enabled hacking
articles.content_orig:
After discovery of severe bug in the PHP programming language, executives warn of ‘vulnerability tsunami’
Leaders in cybersecurity are sounding the alarm after the discovery of a major vulnerability this week. They are predicting that artificial intelligence tools will expose more fundamental weaknesses in global internet infrastructure in the months to come.
“I no longer think we’re going to be able to patch all bugs,” said Sam Altman on Thursday evening, joining the chorus of executives. In the midst of what’s being called “Black October”, for which researchers used AI to help identify critical flaws in a coding language that is used across millions of websites and may have been unpatched for years, tech executives are warning about the ways AI will be used both to identify and exploit security vulnerabilities at an unprecedented scale and pace.
The next few months will see a “vulnerability tsunami”, according to Jason Clinton, Anthropic’s deputy chief information security officer. “There won’t be enough time to patch critical infrastructure,” Clinton said in a post on X on Thursday evening. Marc Benioff, the Salesforce CEO, agreed and called it a “code red”.
AI is uniquely able to find and identify security flaws in a way and at a pace that will feel catastrophic because the security community will not be able to move quickly enough to address them, said Matthew Prince, the Cloudflare CEO. “It’s going to feel like the sky is falling. It’s going to feel like there’s nothing we can do.
“The next two years are going to be incredibly, incredibly, incredibly fraught with new tools that have infinite patience to go look for vulnerabilities across the Internet,” he wrote in a post on X.
While cybersecurity experts have been warning about a “vulnpocalypse”, or the ability for AI to more easily identify security bugs for months, it wasn’t until “Black October” that researchers were able to use AI to find a flaw as fundamental and critical as the one announced on 21 October.
Massive bugs were found in a programming language called PHP, which may have left the millions of websites that run on it vulnerable to hackers for years. Some experts estimated 70% of all the sites on the internet were at risk of hacking.
However, in the same way AI will be used to aid in identifying security vulnerabilities at an unprecedented pace, tech leaders worry it’ll also be used by malicious actors to exploit those bugs at an unprecedented pace.
Attempts to exploit the PHP vulnerability have already begun .
After the vulnerabilities were announced, government and private websites across the US and UK temporarily took down their sites to patch the bugs. The US National Security Agency (NSA) issued an alert recommending any site that runs on PHP implement the patches immediately. Malicious cyberactors may seek to further exploit these bugs to access servers without authorization, the NSA said.
“Such an access vector could help attackers steal sensitive data, disrupt services or move deeper into a network,” the warning read.
after newsletter promotion
In a post on X, Prince said CloudFlare, a security provider, had seen evidence of thousands of people trying to exploit the PHP flaws in the 10 hours before it was announced.
“That jumped to tens of thousands in the 45 minutes post announcement, hundreds of thousands within 2 hours, and millions now,” he wrote.
In a blogpost, researchers at AI security platform Wiz said that this was “among the most severe vulnerabilities discovered in PHP, and arguably in software history”.
“The underlying flaws had been present for decades, but demonstrating their exploitability required an exceptionally complex chain of steps, at the edge of what human researchers could practically achieve,” they wrote.

articles.title_orig: In hunt for Starlink alternative, Ukraine partners with Nokia and satellite maker ICEYE
articles.title_zh: In hunt for Starlink alternative, Ukraine partners with Nokia and satellite maker ICEYE
articles.content_orig:
After SpaceX restricted use of its Starlink and Starshield satellite internet services in Ukraine, causing fast-moving drones to disconnect and drop out of the sky, Kyiv is looking for alternatives.
Ukraine's Ministry of Defense said on Thursday that it has signed a letter of intent to develop new defense and satellite communication capabilities in partnership with Finnish tech companies Nokia and ICEYE, which makes satellites.
"Modern warfare has proven that reliable communications are a matter of national security," Ukraine President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said in a statement . "We must all rely on capabilities that we can control."
Zelenskyy also announced a partnership with Norway this week to jointly develop air defense and communications systems that could serve as an alternative to Starshield.
Chad Anderson, founder and CEO of venture capital firm Space Capital, said such an alternative could be "two to three years away" and that "matching Starlink's scale is a longer road."
SpaceX has around around 11,000 satellites in orbit, according to data tracked by astronomer Jonathan McDowell .
Anderson said Starshield may be an even tougher service to replace. "The Pentagon's own contracting documents say SpaceX is the only provider that can meet some of its needs through 2026. Capital isn't the constraint any more. Launch is."
Even Starlink competitors have relied on SpaceX launches to put their satellites in orbit.
As of Friday, Ukraine officials said the country is still experiencing restrictions on Starlink, which cut connectivity for drones or other aircraft traveling at speeds over 100 mph.
Both the Trump administration and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk have shirked responsibility for the unannounced Starlink service changes that Ukraine reported more than a week ago. President Donald Trump told reporters at the White House on Friday that he would call on Musk to lift the restrictions.
SpaceX executives didn't respond to a request for comment.
Lawmakers in the U.S. from both parties are calling for a formal probe of Musk and SpaceX regarding the alleged unilateral changes the company made to its services in Ukraine.
Jay Shambaugh, a senior fellow at Brookings and professor of economics and international affairs at George Washington University, told CNBC in an email that the sudden Starlink changes are "part of a pattern since Trump came back into office of the United States acting as an unreliable ally."
Shambaugh cautioned that, "over time, that can reduce U.S. exports to the EU if those countries don't want to be dependent on something where the U.S. can cut them off."
Rivals to Starlink are on the horizon, including Amazon's Leo , France's Eutelsat and a forthcoming service from Jeff Bezos' Blue Origin called TeraWave , which has yet to deploy its first satellites.
Beyond Ukraine, several countries are looking into sovereign satellite communications systems. The EU is building IRIS² , a constellation of hundreds of satellites, but its first launches aren't expected until 2029.
Since Russia's invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, venture and private equity investors have poured about $8 billion into Starlink and Starshield alternatives, according to research by Anderson, whose firm tracks industry deals. About $3.9 billion of that funding has gone to potential Starlink competitors, mostly Spacesail and China SatNet.
Virginia Burger, senior defense policy analyst with the Project on Government Oversight, told CNBC in an interview that the problem today is there's no drop-in replacement for Starlink, and combat is moving more into "unmanned systems, drone warfare and other systems that require high-speed internet."
— CNBC's Annie Palmer contributed reporting.

articles.title_zh: Anthropic Is Racing to Price Its IPO Before the Thanksgiving Dealmaking Freeze
articles.content_orig:
Anthropic is gearing up for one of the largest initial public offerings (IPOs) in history, and its public debut could make waves across the broader stock market. Investors probably won't have to wait long for the company's IPO and the resulting fervor.
The company is reportedly aiming to carry out its public debut before Thanksgiving, getting ahead of the informal freeze on dealmaking that tends to immediately precede and follow the holiday. While it's possible that the public debut could slip into early December, itself a popular window for companies going public, signs point to the company conducting its IPO in mid-November.
Image source: Getty Images.
In June, Space Exploration Technologies had its IPO and listed its first batch of publicly available stock at a price of $135 per share. The listing price valued the company at $1.77 trillion -- a level that made SpaceX's IPO the largest ever. While there were expectations that Anthropic would price its stock at a level that would value the company at roughly $2 trillion and set a new valuation record, that's now looking less likely.
NASDAQ · As of 4:00 PM ET 10/23/26
Following some recent volatility for the broader market, concerns about valuations in the artificial intelligence (AI) industry, and updates on Anthropic's business momentum, many analysts expect the company to debut at a valuation of roughly $1.5 trillion. Some estimates suggest that the company could be valued as low as $1.2 trillion at its IPO.
According to a leaked draft version of the company's IPO prospectus, Anthropic generated roughly $16.3 billion in sales across this year's first half -- up from sales of roughly $1.1 billion across the same period last year. That's incredible growth and reflects surging demand for the company's Claude AI software suite, which offers top-tier tools for coding, analysis, and other forms of content generation. On the other hand, the business posted a loss of roughly $80.7 billion in the first half of 2026.
Investors also took a measured approach to reports about the company's third-quarter performance, which suggested that sales in the period had increased 45% on a sequential basis to reach $16.8 billion. While that still represents an incredible rate of growth, some analysts had been expecting the rate of expansion to be even stronger given the momentum across the first half of the year.
Even though Anthropic is unlikely to dethrone SpaceX in terms of IPO size, there's still a good chance that the company will conduct a successful public debut next month. With the company using lots of cash as it spends on compute resources and scales rapidly, going public will provide the AI leader with an influx of capital that can be used to fuel its growth.

Now that the first folding iPhone has launched, we’ll find out quickly what can go wrong.
The iPhone Duo officially goes on sale today, but a few units already have broken screens. According to posts on Reddit about the affected units, the issue appears to be happening at a similar spot on all of them: Some kind of problem shows up on the inner screen along the hinge and a strange bright line (or lines) across the right side of the display.
Here’s how one user in Australia described what happened to their phone:
Had my iPhone Duo for about six hours and had probably opened it fewer than 20 times.
I was showing it to a friend, and as I opened it, I felt something around the internal hinge, underneath the screen.
As I continued opening it, I heard an audible crack, and the screen broke right along the hinge.
There were no marks or damage on the inner screen’s surface or the external hinge to suggest anything had been caught or damaged.
The user said that the Apple Store replaced their phone with “a brand-new one on the spot.”
A post showing an image of another broken screen includes a video in a comment demonstrating yet another.
And a separate Reddit thread collected other pictures of affected Duos.
Apple didn’t immediately reply to a request for comment.

By John Wilkerson and Damian Garde
John writes about the politics of health care, and he is the author of the twice-weekly D.C. Diagnosis newsletter . You can reach John on Signal at John_Wilkerson.07.
Damian covers the global drug industry and contributes to STAT’s industry-leading events. You can reach Damian on Signal at damiangarde.67.
WASHINGTON — The Trump administration late on Thursday proposed a rule that would severely restrict future U.S. investment in the Chinese biotech sector but still allow American drugmakers to buy the rights to medicines invented in the country.
The Treasury Department proposed the rule to implement a law, called the Comprehensive Outbound Investment National Security Act, that restricts U.S. investment in industries of concern to national security. The department added biotechnology to the list of industries subject to COINS restrictions, joining the likes of semiconductors, artificial intelligence, and quantum technology.
The proposal would prohibit U.S. companies from entering financial transactions with Chinese biotech companies or Chinese manufacturers of biotechnology-related equipment and tools, according to the research firm Veda.

articles.title_orig: Mother drowns trying to save sons during Bahamas snorkeling trip
articles.title_zh: Mother drowns trying to save sons during Bahamas snorkeling trip
articles.content_orig:
Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged in Please refresh your browser to be logged in
Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.
A British woman has drowned after trying to rescue her two sons who were swept away while snorkelling in the Bahamas .
The 36-year-old was holidaying with her husband and children, and had gone on an expedition off the southern end of Bimini on Tuesday morning when powerful currents took hold of the boys.
In a desperate attempt to rescue them, the unnamed woman was also carried off, the Royal Bahamas Police Force said.
Her children were pulled out from the water in time, but their mother, who was taken to North Bimini Ferry Dock, was unresponsive and was later pronounced dead in hospital.
Linty Stuart, the owner of L&A Water Taxi, told the Bahamian broadcaster ZNS that he captained the boat that pulled the family from the water after his crew spotted “frantic hands waving in the distance”.
“I immediately went to see what they [crew members] were calling me for,” he recalled. “I saw them pointing towards the west side. I saw two boys and their mother.”
Stuart added that the strong currents made the recovery efforts “extremely difficult” and by the time they got to her, she was already “face down” in the water.
“At least a 7ft to 8ft wave... almost turned the whole vessel over... it shot me down,” he added about the challenging conditions. “Everything happened really, really fast. It’s a shock.”
Footage shared by the broadcaster shows heroic bystanders rushing to the victim’s aid.
Her sons watched in horror as people tried to resuscitate their mother before first responders eventually arrived at the scene as the boat docked.
A post-mortem examination will now take place to determine the cause of death, but police have ruled out foul play.
“According to the preliminary report, shortly after 10am, officers at the Alice Town Police Station received information that a female was unresponsive at the North Bimini Ferry Dock,” the force said in a statement.
“Officers responded and, upon arrival, learned that the woman had been transported to the local clinic for medical attention, where she was subsequently pronounced dead by a local doctor despite efforts to save her life.
“Preliminary information indicates that the deceased was snorkelling with her husband and two sons near the southern point of the island when a strong current reportedly swept both children away.
“In an attempt to rescue her sons, the woman was also swept awat. She was later rescued and transported to the ferry dock, where CPR was reportedly administered.”
The Independent has contacted the Foreign Office for a statement.

articles.title_orig: AI agents are roaming around consumers' bank accounts, and banks aren't happy about it
articles.title_zh: AI agents are roaming around consumers' bank accounts, and banks aren't happy about it
articles.content_orig:
Add Axios as your preferred source to
see more of our stories on Google.
Illustration: Sarah Grillo/Axios. Stock: Getty Images
Major U.S. banks are detecting unauthorized third-party AI agents operating inside customer accounts, with some agents attempting to take actions that appear to be independent of user instructions, sources tell Axios.
Why it matters: AI agents are becoming a nightmare for America's banks, making their way into banking systems faster than financial institutions can respond.
Driving the news: Banks including Morgan Stanley, Bank of America, JPMorgan, Wells Fargo and others are racing to contain agent risks. Some are aware of unauthorized access, people familiar with the issue said.
What they're saying: Bank executives described the situation as horrifying, with one official saying the industry has grave concerns about agents gaining access to customer accounts and taking steps that could impact user finances.
State of play: The concerns are at the root of the decision by several banks to restrict third-party AI agent access, the people said.
Zoom out: Most banks have authorized or are moving in the direction of allowing read-only access , which should allow agents to see customer financial information without taking action.
Reality check: Several industry and bank executives told Axios they recognize the need to find a middle-ground with AI agents.
Threat level: Many banks are broadly not able to parse whether agent account activity is user-directed, sources said.
What we're watching: On one hand, banks are best positioned to respond to the threats and opportunities of AI given their cash on hand and experience as critical infrastructure.
The bottom line: The rapid pace of AI advancement is becoming a security nightmare for America's financial institutions.
